newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian bombs shatter myth that cities are safe.
newsitem.headline: Algerian bombs shatter myth that cities are safe.

text.p: In one of the world's bloodiest undeclared wars, days of bomb attacks have brought Algeria's Moslem fundamentalist conflict back to the heart of the Algerian capital.
Two more bombs on Wednesday ripped through the centre of Algeria's most important military town Blida, 50 km (30 miles) to the south.

"The blasts have shattered the perception that the cities are safer, after the massacres in the villages at the start of (the Moslem fasting month) Ramadan," said one European political analyst by phone. "And the violence will certainly continue."
Ramadan began on January 10. At least 160 people have since died, Algerian newspapers say. Massacres in isolated villages marked the start of the month. Then bombs hit Algiers and Blida.
"The violence was expected during Ramadan, as in previous years. What makes this year different is the sheer intensity, bloodiness, and certainty it will continue," the analyst said.

Algeria's radical Armed Islamic Group (GIA) had promised to intensify what it has termed its "holy war" during Ramadan, threatening a 50-bomb campaign. Besides bombs which killed, at least 17 more have been defused in the past three weeks.
GIA leader Antar Zouabri, in a statement displayed in Algiers, vowed: "We have the means and the men to punish all those who are not on our side."
Diplomats see the statement as the only explanation for bombs in markets and poor districts normally home to the jobless young, many with fundamentalist leanings.

On Wednesday, the independent Algerian paper El Watan said of what it termed "murderous madness": "There is no explanation (for this), from citizens or from experts on the motivation or logic of war."

It is five years since the authorities scrapped a general election which Islamists were poised to win. Violence erupted and about 60,000 people have died. Women, children, foreigners have all been sucked into the whirlpool of bloodshed.

Diplomats say the violence has eroded political support for the Islamists which saw rallies attract over 100,000 supporters for the now banned Islamic Salvation Front and massive protests in city streets. The likelihood of mass unrest has diminished.

"The way things are going right now, they (the authorities) are good for another five years. But so is the opposition. There is evidence they are being supported from outside, by Afghan rebels and others," one diplomat said, without elaborating.
Police in Germany and France this week searched for Islamic militants suspected of acquiring explosives for the GIA. Algiers has also accused Iran and Sudan of supporting Moslem radicals.

Diplomatic sources in Algiers say the latest bloodshed, in what one called "the madness of Algeria", could only produce more violence -- a military-security crackdown, and a response from the armed groups.
"The authorities are divided. President (Liamine) Zeroual has been for some sort of negotiated settlement, while others -- the 'eradicators' -- want a military solution," one said.
"The upsurge of violence plays into the hardliners' hands. In the short term it makes talks or negotiations less likely."
Another diplomatic source told Reuters he saw no change in government policy because of the violence. Nor did he believe a general election, promised within months, would bring a change.
"When we had the presidential election, then the referendum on the constitution last year, people expected change. There has been little. I can't see elections altering anything quickly."
On Wednesday, a Canadian diplomatic source said the embassy was recommending Ottawa to tell anyone who didn't have to visit Algeria to stay away, especially for the next two months.
One diplomat said that after an increase of foreign visitors last year, those who came now were "diplomats who are heavily guarded or oilmen who are also heavily guarded, few others".
One analyst said people "deeply feel the government has failed to...ensure a minimum level of security...they ask why bombers wander freely in streets and where they get explosives."
The legal Islamist party Hamas told the authorities "to assume their entire responsibilities" for Algerians' security.
The Algerian cabinet met on Wednesday but did not discuss the bomb attacks, focusing solely on conditions for retirement, according to a report by the official Algerian news agency APS.
But earlier the government, through Interior Minister Mustapha Ben Mansour, told an already wary population to increase vigilance, admitting "it is difficult to ward off bomb attacks".
He was not quoted any longer as mentioning the long-stated government claims that only "residual terrorism" now remains.
